claims.text: The nanoparticles contain Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Ni in equiatomic proportions of approximately 20 at.% each.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles are a single-phase solid solution.
Rapid inert-gas condensation produces CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles with high grain-boundary density.
Rapid inert-gas condensation produces CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles with high twin-boundary density.
Chemical reduction produces larger and more coherent CoCrFeMnNi grains than rapid inert-gas condensation.
Chemical reduction produces CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles with lower grain- and twin-boundary density.
Grain boundaries provide fast atomic-diffusion channels.
Twin boundaries provide fast atomic-diffusion channels.
A greater grain- and twin-boundary density accelerates atomic migration in CoCrFeMnNi nanoparticles.
Accelerated defect-mediated atomic migration promotes elemental segregation.
Accelerated defect-mediated atomic migration promotes structural coarsening.
Reducing grain- and twin-boundary density limits atomic diffusion.
Limiting diffusion preserves the chemically homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
After thermal exposure from 473 to 1923 K, the lower-boundary-density nanoparticles will show less phase segregation than the higher-boundary-density nanoparticles.
After thermal exposure from 473 to 1923 K, the lower-boundary-density nanoparticles will show less chemical inhomogeneity than the higher-boundary-density nanoparticles.
After thermal exposure from 473 to 1923 K, the higher-boundary-density nanoparticles will undergo more structural coarsening.
An inert atmosphere excludes oxidation as an extrinsic contributor to the observed stability differences.
If bulk diffusion dominates at the highest temperatures, stability differences between the two boundary-density variants will become less pronounced.
